text: Hi, how's it going? I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT, and my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment, and I'm pretty much a homebody. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, music, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

Well, when it comes to healthy food, Koreans are really serious about it. The first thing that comes to mind is kimchi. It's packed with good bacteria, and we eat it with almost every meal. We also eat a lot of rice with vegetables, like bibimbap, and soups with tofu or seaweed. My friend says seaweed soup is the best thing for your body. And when it's hot outside, people eat samgyetang, which is chicken soup with ginseng. It sounds strange, but it really works! As for where people buy it, most folks go to a big supermarket or a traditional market. Honestly, I like the traditional market better, because the vegetables are fresh and cheap. These days, a lot of people order groceries online, and they show up at your door before dawn. That's pretty convenient.

To be honest, I wasn't always careful about my health. I sit at a desk all day, drink way too much coffee, and I'm not a gym guy at all. But two years ago, my checkup results came back, and the doctor said my cholesterol was a little high. That was a wake-up call. So I made a few small changes. First, I take the stairs at work, even though my office is on the 7th floor! Second, my friend and I take a walk along a nearby beach after dinner, at least three times a week. And I cut back on late-night snacks, which was the hardest part. At my next checkup, the numbers were back to normal. I felt so proud of myself. I still drink my coffee, of course, but now I keep it to three cups a day. Well, maybe four.

Things have changed a lot. When I was a kid, people mostly stayed healthy by eating well at home. My mom made chicken soup whenever someone caught a cold. There was always somebody telling me to wear a jacket and wash my hands! And if you felt sick, you just drank hot water and went to bed early. Nobody went to a gym back then. You stayed in shape by playing outside all day. These days, it's a whole different story. People use apps and smartwatches to count their steps and track their sleep. Gyms and yoga studios are everywhere, and people take vitamins and protein shakes. I even wear a smartwatch myself, and it buzzes at me when I sit too long. So I'd say we used to rely on family habits, and now we rely on technology.

As a coffee lover, I could talk about this all day. My favorite place is a small roastery cafe right by the sea in my city. From the outside, it looks like an old warehouse. But when you walk in, you smell fresh roasted beans, and it just makes you feel good. What makes it special is that the owner roasts the beans himself. He's a quiet guy with a gray beard, and he knows exactly what I like. When I walk in, he says, "The usual?" That's the moment I feel like a regular. There's also a big window facing the ocean, so you can watch the ships go by while you sip your coffee. I go there almost every weekend. It's the one place where I can really slow down.

Well, my routine at a coffee shop is pretty much the same every time. I order a hot americano, and if I'm feeling a little greedy, a piece of cheesecake too. Then I find a seat by the window. Most of the time, I read. I'm kind of into mystery novels these days, so I bring one with me. Once I start reading, I lose track of time. Sometimes I open my laptop and catch up on emails, but I try not to do too much work there. I mean, it's my day off! Now and then, I meet a friend or two, and we just talk for hours. The thing I love most is the background music. I don't know why, but I enjoy reading more with music on. Honestly, a good coffee shop is like a second home to me.

One time at my favorite cafe, I had a total heart attack moment. It was a Saturday afternoon, and I was working on a report on my laptop. I stood up to grab a napkin, and I bumped the table with my knee. My latte tipped over, and it went right toward my laptop! Everything happened in slow motion. I grabbed the laptop with both hands and lifted it up in the air, like I was holding a trophy. The coffee went all over the table and my pants, but the laptop was totally fine! People around me were staring. I wanted to disappear. But the owner came running with a pile of towels, and he said, "Don't worry, it happens to everyone!" He cleaned up the whole mess, and he even made me a new latte for free. I couldn't help but laugh. After that day, I always keep my cup on the far side of the table.

Music is a big part of my life. I listen to it every day, on my way to work, at my desk, and before bed. I'm mostly into rock and pop, but I also listen to calm piano music when I need to focus. My all-time favorite is this one K-pop group. I know almost every song by heart. What I love about them is the voice and the melody. They have this way of making a sad song feel warm, if that makes sense. Whenever I'm stressed out at work, I put on my headphones and play one of their songs, and I feel better in about three minutes. I'm also a bit of a nerd about it. I read about the band and watch their interviews. Honestly, I don't think I could live without music.

I got into music because of my family. When I was a kid, everyone in the house had their own cassette tapes. The house was always full of music, so I had no choice but to listen! At first, I only heard ballads and dance songs that the others liked. I even knew all the lyrics to songs for teenage girls, which is kind of embarrassing now. Then in middle school, I got my own cassette player, and I started picking my own music. That's when I found rock. I listened to loud guitar music for years. These days, my taste has calmed down. I still love rock, but I also enjoy quiet piano music and acoustic songs. I guess I got older and mellower. But I'm still thankful to my family for starting it all.

Yes, and it was a night I'll never forget. A few years ago, I went to a K-pop concert in Seoul with a friend. It was an outdoor concert, and I'd been waiting for it for months. But on the day of the show, it started pouring rain. We stood there in cheap raincoats, soaked from head to toe. I thought, "This is going to be a disaster." But then the band came out, and nobody cared about the rain anymore. When they played my favorite song, everyone sang along at the top of their lungs. I got goosebumps. I looked over at my friend, and my friend was crying and laughing at the same time. We were completely soaked, but it was the happiest night. I think a live show hits you in a way that a recording never can.

Hello, I'd like to make an appointment for a haircut. I have an important meeting in two days, so I'd like to come in by tomorrow afternoon if possible. I have a few questions. First, do you have any openings tomorrow afternoon?. Okay, how about three o'clock? Is that time available?. Great. And how long will the haircut take? I have another appointment afterward, so I want to make sure I'm not late.. Got it. Also, which stylist will be cutting my hair? I'd like someone who's good with short, simple cuts.. One last thing: how much is a men's haircut?. Perfect. I'll see you tomorrow at three. Thank you so much!

Hello, I just got a haircut at your salon about an hour ago. I'm sorry to bother you, but I'm not happy with how it turned out. I asked for a short, neat cut on the sides, but it's way too short, and the left side is higher than the right. I have an important meeting tomorrow, so I'm kind of freaking out. I don't want to be rude, but I was wondering if there's anything you can do. Could the stylist take a look and fix it?. And if it can't be fixed, would it be possible to get a discount or a refund?. Okay. Can I come back in this evening?. Thank you so much for understanding. I really appreciate it.

Oh, I have a great one. When I was about ten years old, my mom took me to the hair salon. I was supposed to get a simple haircut. But some relatives came along, and all of them started giving opinions. "Make it short!" "No, keep it long!" The poor hairdresser didn't know what to do. In the end, they all agreed on something called a bowl cut. I walked out looking like a mushroom! At school the next day, my friends laughed at me for a week. I was so embarrassed, I wore a hat everywhere. My relatives just said, "You look so cute!" Looking back, it's a funny story, and we still joke about it every New Year's. Now I always tell the stylist exactly what I want. And I go to the salon alone!

Well, when something breaks at home, the first thing I do is search for it online. Last month, our kitchen sink started leaking. I watched a video on YouTube, bought a new part, and fixed it myself in about 20 minutes. Okay, the first time, I made it worse. Water went everywhere, and my family just looked at me. But in the end, I got it done. If I can't fix it, I use an app to call a repairman. My parents were totally different. When something broke, my dad just picked up his toolbox and started fixing it. He was handy with everything, and if he couldn't fix it, he called a neighbor. They didn't have the Internet, so they relied on experience and word of mouth. So I'd say the difference is this: they used their hands and their neighbors, and I use my phone. My dad still thinks my way is a bit lazy!

There are a few problems that come up a lot when people rent a home. The biggest one is probably the deposit. In Korea, you often pay a huge deposit when you rent, and some landlords don't give it back on time. That happens because the landlord is short on cash, or the next tenant hasn't shown up yet. Another common issue is repairs. Something breaks, like the heater or a faucet, and the landlord says, "That's not my problem." There's also noise from the neighbors, and sometimes mold on the walls in the summer. So how do people solve these problems? First, they read the contract very carefully before signing. Second, they take photos of everything when they move in, so no one can argue later. And if things go wrong, people talk to the landlord politely first, and if that doesn't work, they ask for help from a real estate agent or a legal office. I think the key is to put everything in writing.
